sentences.text: Taurovenator is a genus of dinosaur belonging to the family Carcharodontosauridae, a group of large theropods.
It is classified as a very large carcharodontosaurid and ranks among the largest known theropod dinosaurs and one of the biggest terrestrial carnivores.
Estimates based on comparisons with related species suggest the skull of Taurovenator was around 135 cm long.
The animal possessed a postorbital bone that projected outward like a horn, a trait distinct from other carcharodontosaurids, measuring 3-4 cm in height and 2-3 cm in diameter.

Its neck vertebrae featured prominent neural spines with flange-like dorsal tips, forming an interlocking structure resembling overlapping roof tiles, with one dorsal vertebra reaching a height of 52 cm.

However, other researchers noted that based on an orbital section length of 12 centimeters, the animal might be considered a medium-sized theropod, describing the orbital horn as relatively robust but small and rounded.
A unique feature of this dinosaur was a horn-like projection on its postorbital bone, distinct from other members of its family.
Its neck vertebrae formed a unique interlocking complex resembling overlapping roof tiles.
Fossilized pollen from the same rock layers indicates the environment supported a diverse plant community including ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms.
The genus Taurovenator was named by Motta and colleagues in 2016.
The type species of the genus is Taurovenator violantei.

Initially, the animal was known only from a single postorbital bone unearthed by Matias Motta in 2005 from the lower member of the Huincul Formation on Violante Farm in Rio Negro Province, Argentina, specifically at Rancho Violante on the shores of Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexía.
In 2024, a previously undescribed partial skeleton found at the same site was referred to Taurovenator.
Motta et al. (2016) classified Taurovenator as a derived member of Carcharodontosauridae, closely related to Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Mapusaurus.
Fossils were found in the Huincul Formation, which consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash, within a braided river drainage system.
The Paleobi Database records the time range of Taurovenator as the Albian, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago, differing from other estimates.

Some paleontologists have debated whether Taurovenator is synonymous with the genus Mapusaurus. Coria et al. (2019) suggested Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus because their original distinguishing features were shared, arguing that its unique features were shared with Mapusaurus. Researcher Mickey Mortimer believed Taurovenator was synonymous with Mapusaurus due to insufficient diagnostic material, and it has been suggested that Taurovenator is a synonym of Mapusaurus.
However, differences in stratigraphic layers suggest Taurovenator, Meraxes, and Mapusaurus may not have lived at the same time, supporting Taurovenator's validity.
A 2025 study by Cau and Paterna debated the classification of Taurovenator, placing it outside the family Carcharodontosauridae.
